faqs.question: What is the fastest-growing privacy plant for Georgia?
faqs.answer: Green Giant Arborvitae is the fastest-growing privacy plant for Georgia yards, adding 3–5 feet per year until it reaches its mature height of 30–40 feet. It tolerates Georgia's clay soil and humidity better than Leyland Cypress and resists most of the disease issues that affect other screening evergreens.

faqs.question: How far apart should I plant privacy trees?
faqs.answer: Space most privacy trees and shrubs 5–8 feet apart on center for a solid screen within 3–5 years, or 3–4 feet apart for a faster, denser wall of foliage. Exact spacing depends on the mature width of the variety, so check each plant's spec sheet before laying out your row.

faqs.question: What flowering shrubs bloom the longest in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Encore Azaleas and Knock Out Roses bloom the longest of any flowering shrub in Georgia, flowering in spring, summer, and fall rather than a single short window. Reblooming Hydrangeas like Endless Summer and Limelight also extend color from early summer into fall.

faqs.question: When should I plant flowering shrubs in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Fall (October–November) is the best time to plant flowering shrubs in Georgia because cooler air temperatures reduce transplant stress while the still-warm soil lets roots establish before spring growth. Late winter through early spring is the next-best window.

faqs.question: What is the best small yard tree for Georgia?
faqs.answer: Eastern Redbud and Crape Myrtle are the best small yard trees for Georgia, typically staying under 25 feet tall while delivering heavy spring or summer bloom. Both tolerate clay soil, full sun to part shade, and Georgia's humid summers without special care.

faqs.question: How long does it take a tree to reach mature height?
faqs.answer: Most fast-growing trees reach mature height in Georgia within 10–15 years, while slower-growing ornamentals like Japanese Maple can take 20+ years. Growth rate depends on species, soil, sun exposure, and watering during the establishment period.

faqs.question: What plants grow best in Georgia clay soil?
faqs.answer: Azaleas, Hydrangeas, Loropetalum, Black-Eyed Susan, and Muscadine grapes grow best in Georgia clay soil once organic matter is worked into the planting hole. Native species like American Beautyberry and Virginia Sweetspire tolerate clay without any soil amendment at all.

faqs.question: What USDA zone is most of Georgia in?
faqs.answer: Most of Georgia falls in USDA Hardiness Zone 7b–8a, meaning average annual minimum temperatures range from 5°F to 15°F. BB Blossoms selects every plant in this collection to reliably survive and thrive within that zone range.

faqs.question: What fruit trees grow well in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Peach, fig, apple, pear, blueberry, and muscadine grape all grow well in Georgia when matched to the right chill-hour requirement for your zone. Rabbiteye Blueberries and Brown Turkey Figs are especially reliable because they tolerate Georgia's clay soil and humid summers with minimal spraying.

faqs.question: Do I need two fruit trees to get fruit?
faqs.answer: Most apple, pear, and blueberry varieties need a second, different variety nearby for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set, while fig and some peach varieties are self-fertile and produce fruit alone. Check each plant's spec sheet for pollination requirements before buying just one.

faqs.question: What is the easiest houseplant to keep alive?
faqs.answer: Pothos and Snake Plant are the easiest houseplants to keep alive because both tolerate low light, irregular watering, and typical indoor humidity without special care. They're a reliable starting point for anyone new to indoor plants.

faqs.question: How often should I water indoor plants?
faqs.answer: Most houseplants should be watered every 7–10 days, letting the top inch or two of soil dry out between waterings to prevent root rot. Succulents and snake plants need water even less often — roughly every 2–3 weeks.

intro: Ornamental grasses add movement, texture, and low-maintenance structure to Georgia landscapes, from small border grasses to tall privacy screens. Most varieties are drought-tolerant once established and require only an annual cutback.

faqs.question: When should ornamental grasses be cut back?
faqs.answer: Cut ornamental grasses back to 4–6 inches in late winter (February in Georgia) before new spring growth emerges. Cutting back any earlier removes winter interest and cold-season habitat for beneficial insects.

faqs.question: Are ornamental grasses low maintenance?
faqs.answer: Yes — most ornamental grasses are low maintenance once established, needing only an annual cutback, occasional division every 3–4 years, and little to no supplemental watering or fertilizing in Georgia's climate.

faqs.question: What perennials come back every year in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Coneflower, Black-Eyed Susan, Daylily, Salvia, and Hosta are among the most reliable perennials that return every year in Georgia, surviving both summer heat and winter cold in Zone 8a without needing to be dug up.

faqs.question: Do perennials need to be replanted every year?
faqs.answer: No — unlike annuals, perennials do not need to be replanted every year. Their root systems survive winter dormancy and regrow each spring, though many benefit from dividing every 3–4 years to stay vigorous.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an annual and a perennial?
faqs.answer: An annual completes its life cycle in one growing season and must be replanted each year, while a perennial regrows from the same root system for multiple years. Annuals typically bloom longer and more intensely in a single season than most perennials.

faqs.question: When should I plant summer annuals in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Plant summer annuals in Georgia after the last frost date, typically mid-to-late April in the Atlanta metro area, once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 50°F.
